title: The Cleveland Torso Murders
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Cleveland Torso Murders of the 1930s, a series of dismemberment killings around Kingsbury Run in Cleveland, Ohio. They walk through the victims, including the Lady of the Lake, the men found in 1935, Flo Polillo, the tattooed unidentified man shown in a death mask at the Great Lakes Exposition, and later victims. They cover the investigation led by Peter Morillo, the involvement of public safety director Elliott Ness, the Torso Clinic conference, the Sandusky dog-and-leg lead, the raid and burning of the Kingsbury Run shantytown, the wrongful confession and death of Frank Dolezal, and Ness's secret detention of a suspect, "Gay Lord Sondheim," identified by later writers as surgeon Francis Edward Sweeney. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from John Goodman, a clarinet repair technician in Greensboro, North Carolina, who listened to the Korean fan death episode.

segments.title: Intro and framing of the Torso murders
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about gruesome true crime from the 1930s and introduce the Cleveland Torso murders as unsolved serial killings with a famous investigator.

segments.title: Lady of the Lake and the first victims
segments.summary: A woman's torso washes up on Lake Erie in September 1934 without a head or lower legs, later called the Lady of the Lake. Two years later two dismembered men are found near Kingsbury Run; one is identified as Edward Andrewski, a petty thief.

segments.title: Kingsbury Run and the Hooverville
segments.summary: Kingsbury Run is described as a riverbed used as an industrial dumping ground that became a Depression-era shantytown. Flo Polillo's dismembered body is found in January 1936, and a fourth victim's head is found in the Cuyahoga River in June 1936.

segments.title: Tattooed man and the death mask
segments.summary: Police make a death mask and a tattoo map of an unidentified tattooed man and display them at the Great Lakes Exposition in 1936. He was never identified.

segments.title: Later victims and the victim count
segments.summary: Hosts list later victims, including skeletal remains identified as Rose Wallace, a victim with a heart removed, and a victim with morphine in her system. The last canonical victims were found in August 1938.

segments.title: Break and tease
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and tease the famous investigator's identity.

segments.title: Elliott Ness joins the case
segments.summary: Elliott Ness, former head of the Untouchables and alcohol tax investigator, is named public safety director of Cleveland and becomes the public face of the investigation alongside lead detective Peter Morillo.

segments.title: Torso Clinic and the killer profile
segments.summary: Coroner A. J. Pierce convenes a conference dubbed the Torso Clinic, where a profile is offered: a man who blends in, is powerful, and has anatomical skill. Hosts discuss evidence of blood drainage and the need for a hidden dismemberment site.

segments.title: Press involvement, undercover work, and the Sandusky leg
segments.summary: Ness and others bring the press into a secret effort with undercover operatives. Police chase a lead after a dog appears in Sandusky with a human leg, which turns out to be from a surgery. The lead goes nowhere, and public pressure mounts.

segments.title: Kingsbury Run raid, fire, and Frank Dolezal
segments.summary: Ness orders the Kingsbury Run camps raided and burned, which angers the public, though murders stop afterward. Frank Dolezal, a bricklayer, is arrested and confesses, then dies in his cell; his confession is believed coerced and no serious scholar considers him the killer. Ness also orders searches under the guise of fire code inspections.

segments.title: Gay Lord Sondheim and Francis Sweeney
segments.summary: Ness secretly holds a suspect called Gay Lord Sondheim for two weeks without charge and has him interrogated and given a polygraph by Leonard Keeler. Later writers identify him as Dr. Francis Edward Sweeney, a former surgeon with a congressman relative, though no definitive proof exists. Circumstantial evidence includes a 1934 incident in a Broadway doctor's office and a Sandusky veterans' home stay.

segments.title: Competing theories and wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts note competing theories, including multiple killers or copycats, and mention a Black Dahlia-related taunting note they consider unlikely to be connected. They suggest further reading by James Badal and Maryland Bardsley.

segments.title: Listener mail from John Goodman
segments.summary: A listener who repairs musical instruments in Greensboro, North Carolina, writes that he listened to the Korean fan death episode and hoped to get rid of a fan, and shares a laugh with his fiancee. The hosts sign off with the show's email address.
